A GAME OF ANGLES

Welcome to real tennis.

One court. Two players. A few wonderfully unusual rules.

01 · Move and swing

Move the mouse over your half of the floor. Your player accelerates toward it and brakes as he arrives. Roll the wheel toward you for a backswing, then away from you to swing forward. Faster wheel movement hits harder, with a softer power range and a capped maximum. Choose Calibrate power in Settings → Controls & view, then hit ten comfortable drives to set your normal swing to medium strength. Missed swings do not count; the calibration is saved on this device. Recalibrate or reset it in Settings. You need to meet the ball during that forward stroke; a missed swing is not queued. On touch screens, drag on the court to move, and use the separate racket pad for the stroke.

A centered strike goes straight with more timing leeway. Forehand: late contact goes right and early goes left. Backhand reverses those angles. Contact farther ahead or behind gives more sideways placement, with extra range toward the solid main wall. Centered contact still goes straight. The racket anticipates forehand or backhand from the ball’s bounces and your movement toward the cursor. The elbow bends on the backswing. Contact occurs as the racket reaches sideways across the court; watch the racket rather than trying to time a meter. Both sides have a wider reach and a more forgiving stroke window. Choose Practice: right at me for steady feeds toward your current position, or Practice: left & right for alternating feeds that make you move your feet. Misses automatically start another feed; no points or chases are scored. Choose Match in Change session for scoring. While the ball is coming toward you, swing without clicking for a regular shot. Left-click anywhere on the court to select one drive, or right-click for one lob. A drive hits with more power than a regular return, flies a little flatter and faster, and uses more energy in a match. Practice and the controls tutorial keep your energy full. Click once at any time before contact; you do not need to click while scrolling. Your choice stays set through the backswing and resets to Regular after contact. You can change it before contact. On touch screens, tap Drive or Lob. Wheel speed sets power and body position still affects direction. Drives can hit the net; lobs can fall short or go out. There is no automatic net clearance. When it is your serve, left-click anywhere on the court to start service (or press Space). You can also walk back to the central dedans opening to collect a fresh ball; your player bends to pick it up, then walks to the service position.

02 · Use the building

Build rallies deep toward the main wall. Match opponents favor that side, with occasional crosscourt shots when space opens up. Groundstrokes have a lower, skidding bounce. Walls and sloping penthouse roofs are in play. The angled tambour changes the rebound. Hit the dedans, grille, or winning gallery for an immediate winner.

03 · Understand a chase

A second bounce on the service end lays a chase instead of scoring a point. After two chases, or one at game point, change ends. The challenger must beat its depth, or hit a winner. The gold line shows the target.

04 · Play a set

15, 30, 40, deuce, advantage. Choose three- or six-game sets and one, best-of-three or best-of-five sets in settings. The initial service end is decided by a racket spin. Choose Bobble, Railroad, Giraffe, Demi-piqué or Side-wall before serving, plus long or short placement. Your player walks behind the second-gallery line, tosses with his left hand, and swings. These are simplified, physically simulated versions of the traditional serves.

EARLY PLAYTEST · Core singles rules, floor and gallery chases, winning openings, two service attempts, and changing ends are included. Court dimensions, ball behavior, serve variety, chase calls, and uncommon law exceptions are still being refined. This is not yet a complete rules simulation.
